schema_doc: counties[fips].rot[rotation_class] = list of cards {s: strategy_id, v: 18 numbers = [est, lo, hi] for each name in `fields` (null = not quantified), f: card flag codes}; county-level flag codes in counties[fips].f; flag text templates in `flags` ({irr},{prcp},{edd},{aws},{c45},{s3p} come from counties[fips].ctx); shared card text (name, why, benefits, gaps, risks, evidence) in `strategies`.
units: USD per acre per year (rotation average over the crops in the rotation)
dollar_year: 2020-2024 nominal (county liability per insured acre 2020-2024; NASS/ERS 2019-2023 for income)
interval_method: 5th-95th percentile over 100 bootstrap refits of the loss model, combined per draw; for scenario cards the envelope over the rotation scenario r = lo..hi
income_method: delta_income_per_ac = change in net return vs the current rotation, $/acre/yr: NASS county yield (2019-2023 each year; state, then same-ERS-region states, then US when suppressed) x NASS state marketing-year price (US when missing) minus USDA ERS Commodity Costs and Returns 'Total, operating costs' per planted acre (region: IA/IL/MN/MO Heartland, KS/NE Prairie Gateway, SD Northern Great Plains; sorghum Prairie Gateway); est = mean of the 5 yearly deltas, lo/hi = min/max over the years under the low/high rotation-yield assumptions. Excludes insurance premiums and indemnities, land, machinery and overhead.

scenario.label: Scenario assumption, not an estimate from the county data: field trials (Bowles et al. 2020) found 14-90% smaller maize drought-year yield losses in diversified rotations. est = trial lower bound (14%); lo = no effect (the county data show no robust effect); hi = trial upper bound (90%).

3+ crop.mix: 1/3 corn + 1/3 soybeans + 1/3 wheat (small grain); corn gets the rotation scenario

with perennial.mix: corn and soybean years only (1/2 + 1/2); hay/alfalfa years are not in the drought bill (no county forage model); corn gets the rotation scenario

strategies.name: Keep current rotation
strategies.description: Your baseline: what your rotation draws from crop insurance for drought, per acre per year.
strategies.why: Baseline. The county's loss model (trained on 2001-2024 RMA drought claims) is applied to every NASA POWER weather year 1981-2024 with today's insured crops; each crop's simulated loss is weighted by its share in your rotation, year by year, so bad years add up correctly.
benefits: No change in equipment, markets or know-how.
gaps: The bill is insured drought loss (RMA cause 'drought') at 2020-2024 coverage and prices; your own uninsured loss can be larger.
Each crop uses the county-average insured loss cost for that crop; field soils and management are not observed.
In the 2021-2024 test the model ranked counties well but under-predicted the 2022 and 2023 regional totals by about half (multi-season droughts).
risks: Climate projections (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, 3 models) raise the regional drought bill by about 78% (SSP2-4.5) to 111% (SSP5-8.5) around 2045 at today's acres and prices.

sources.label: USDA RMA Cause of Loss + Summary of Business (county drought indemnity, liability)
NASA POWER daily weather 1981-2024 (loss-model hazard)
Drought Bill loss model: out-of-time test 2021-2024 (VALIDATION.md)

strategies.name: Rotate: corn-soybean
strategies.description: Grow soybeans every other year; corn follows soybean.
strategies.why: Corn after soybean yields more than corn after corn: about 1.03 t/ha (~16 bu/acre) in randomized trials combined with satellite data (Kluger et al. 2022); Iowa trials found continuous corn 11-28% lower (Al-Kaisi et al. 2015). The bill change uses the county's soybean loss costs for half the acres. For the corn half it adds a SCENARIO, not an estimate: rotated corn loses 14% less in drought years (range 0%-90%), the same assumption as the diversity slider (Bowles et al. 2020).
benefits: Higher corn yield after soybean (the rotation benefit).
Corn after soybean needs less nitrogen fertilizer than corn after corn.
gaps: No trial isolates corn-soybean vs continuous corn in drought years: the drought part is a scenario.
ERS operating costs are not split by rotation; continuous corn usually needs more nitrogen, so the income gain is likely understated.
Insured corn in a county mixes rotations; the continuous-corn bill uses the county average and probably understates continuous-corn losses.
risks: The corn rotation benefit is about 29% smaller in the hottest years than in the coolest (Kluger et al. 2022).
Soybean drought losses (August pod fill) remain; soybean markets and prices.

sources.label: Kluger, Owen & Lobell 2022, Environ. Res. Lett. 17:044066 (corn rotation benefit, smaller in hot years)
Al-Kaisi et al. 2015, Agron. J. (Iowa rotation trials)
Seifert, Roberts & Lobell 2017, Agron. J. (750k fields)
Bowles et al. 2020, One Earth 2:284 (diverse rotations: 14-90% smaller maize drought-year losses)
USDA RMA Cause of Loss + Summary of Business (county drought indemnity, liability)

strategies.income_note: NASS yields x state prices minus USDA ERS operating costs. Continuous-corn yield = county yield minus the rotation benefit: 1.03 t/ha (Kluger 2022; range 2.5% net, Kluger 2025, to 18.5% of CC yield, Al-Kaisi 2015).

strategies.name: Add a small grain: corn-soybean-wheat
strategies.description: A 3-year rotation: 1/3 corn, 1/3 soybeans, 1/3 wheat (or another small grain).
strategies.why: Spreads drought risk across seasons: wheat grows in fall and spring and is harvested by early summer, before the July-August heat that drives corn and soybean drought losses. The bill change combines the county's own simulated wheat loss costs for a third of the acres with a TRIAL-BASED SCENARIO for corn: corn in a 3+ crop rotation loses 14% less in drought years (range 0%-90%; Bowles et al. 2020 found 14-90% across 11 long-term trials). Our county insurance data did not confirm a protective effect of rotation diversity on corn drought losses (no robust estimate; see model/outputs/diversity_effect.json).
benefits: In the Iowa Marsden Farm trial (Davis et al. 2012), 3- and 4-year rotations had 4% higher corn and 9% higher soybean yields than corn-soybean, with 83% less manufactured nitrogen and 88% less herbicide.
A crop that is harvested in early summer avoids the corn silking window.
Breaks corn-soybean pest and weed cycles.
gaps: Our county insurance data did not confirm a protective effect of rotation diversity on corn drought losses (no robust estimate; see model/outputs/diversity_effect.json): the drought benefit shown is the trial range, not a local estimate.
Bowles et al. had no Iowa site; the closest analog (Minnesota, corn-soy vs corn-soy-oat/alfalfa) showed no significant drought-year benefit.
A national satellite study found -3.4% corn yield for 3-year vs corn-soybean rotations (Kluger et al. 2025, observational).
Wheat loss costs come from a May-August weather model; fall-to-spring droughts that hurt winter wheat (e.g. Kansas 2023) are under-predicted, so wheat losses are likely understated.
risks: Rotation benefits for corn shrink in the hottest years (about 29% smaller in the hottest vs coolest temperature quintile, Kluger et al. 2022).
Needs a local market for wheat or oats, and equipment and know-how for a third crop.
Wheat usually earns less per acre than corn: check the income line.

sources.label: Bowles et al. 2020, One Earth 2:284 (diverse rotations: 14-90% smaller maize drought-year losses)
Drought Bill county-data analysis of rotation diversity (no robust effect)
Kluger, Owen & Lobell 2022, Environ. Res. Lett. 17:044066 (corn rotation benefit, smaller in hot years)
Davis et al. 2012, PLoS ONE (Marsden Farm, Iowa)
Kluger, Di Tommaso & Lobell 2025, Environ. Res. Lett.
USDA RMA Cause of Loss + Summary of Business (county drought indemnity, liability)

strategies.income_note: NASS yields x state prices minus USDA ERS operating costs. Rotation yield effect: central 0; range -3.4% corn (Kluger 2025) to +4% corn / +9% soybean (Davis 2012).

strategies.name: Cereal rye cover crop
strategies.description: Plant cereal rye after harvest; terminate it before the next crop.
strategies.why: Living roots over winter protect the soil and can improve infiltration and soil organic matter. Its effect on drought losses is NOT quantified, so the bill is shown unchanged: drought-year evidence is a farmer survey (SARE/CTIC 2012: corn +9.6%, soybean +11.6% after cover crops, self-reported), while controlled studies show no average corn yield change with grass covers (Marcillo & Miguez 2017: 0%) and -4.6% corn after rye in Iowa trials (Pantoja et al. 2015).
strategies.not_quantified: Drought-bill effect not quantified: no controlled evidence on drought-year losses.
benefits: Cuts interrill erosion about 54% and rill erosion about 90% vs no-till without a cover (Kaspar et al. 2001, central Iowa).
Raises water infiltration about 34.8% on average (Basche & DeLonge 2019 meta-analysis).
Raises soil organic carbon about 4% with non-legume covers (He et al. 2025).
Cuts tile-drainage nitrate load about 61% (Kaspar et al. 2007, central Iowa).
Cost-share exists: in 2018 federal and state cover-crop payments ranged from $12 to $92 per acre (USDA ERS EIB-222); some years add a $5/acre crop-insurance premium discount.
gaps: No controlled study isolates cover-crop effects on drought-year insured losses.
The drought-year yield gains are self-reported (SARE/CTIC survey, >750 farmers), not a trial.
Income line = trial yield effects (corn -4.6% to 0%, soybean -3.1% to +0.2%) minus rye seed ($14-16/acre, USDA ERS); seeding, termination passes and cost-share are not included.
risks: In dry areas a cover crop can use spring soil water the next crop needs: in the Central Great Plains wheat after cover crops yielded ~10% less than after fallow, more in dry years (Nielsen et al. 2016).
Terminate early before corn in a dry spring; late termination can cut corn yield.
Fields with 3+ years of cover crops had -5.5% corn and -3.5% soybean yield in a satellite study (Deines et al. 2023), larger after dry springs.

sources.label: SARE/CTIC 2012-13 cover crop survey (farmer-reported; via MSU Extension)
Marcillo & Miguez 2017, J. Soil Water Conserv. (meta-analysis)
Pantoja et al. 2015, SSSAJ (Iowa rye trials)
Kaspar et al. 2001 (erosion; ISU PM 1999)
Basche & DeLonge 2019 (infiltration meta-analysis)
He et al. 2025, npj Sustain. Agric.
Deines et al. 2023, Global Change Biology
USDA ERS EIB-222 (2021) Cover Crop Trends, Programs, and Practices (seed costs, cost-share)

strategies.income_note: yield effects and rye seed cost only (seeding/termination not included)

strategies.name: Swap corn for grain sorghum
strategies.description: Grow grain sorghum in the corn years (e.g. sorghum-soybean).
strategies.why: Sorghum tolerates heat and dry spells better than corn and uses less water: in a 2009-2011 Nebraska rainfed trial it used over 2 inches less water than corn or soybean (UNL CropWatch); K-State reports a yield advantage over corn where yields are below about 80 bu/acre. The bill uses this county's simulated sorghum loss costs and sorghum liability per acre (state-pooled where flagged).
benefits: Lower seed and fertilizer costs than corn (USDA ERS operating costs).
Better water-use efficiency and heat tolerance in dryland, lower-yield fields.
gaps: Part of any bill change comes from lower liability per acre (less insured value), not only fewer losses.
Where much of the corn is irrigated, insured sorghum is mostly dryland, so the swap can even raise the county-average bill: compare like with like on your own fields.
Sorghum insurance history is short in many counties; flagged counties use pooled estimates.
Sorghum operating costs for 2019-2023 are published only for the Prairie Gateway region; used for every state.
risks: Corn has the higher yield ceiling: where water is ample corn usually earns more.
Local elevator access and price basis for sorghum.
Different pests (e.g. sugarcane aphid, birds) and fewer herbicide options than corn.

sources.label: USDA RMA Cause of Loss + Summary of Business (county drought indemnity, liability)
UNL CropWatch, sorghum water use (Rees 2013; reported, not opened)
K-State Agricultural Experiment Station sorghum vs corn reports (reported, not opened)
USDA NASS QuickStats county yields and state prices 2019-2023
USDA ERS Commodity Costs and Returns (operating costs by region)

strategies.income_note: NASS yields x state prices minus USDA ERS operating costs (sorghum costs: Prairie Gateway).

strategies.name: Swap corn for wheat
strategies.description: Grow wheat in the corn years (e.g. wheat-soybean, often with double-crop soybeans).
strategies.why: Where sorghum is not an established insured crop, wheat is the drought-escape option: it grows in fall and spring and is harvested by early summer, before the July-August heat that drives most corn drought losses. The bill uses the county's simulated wheat loss costs and wheat liability per acre.
benefits: Harvest in early summer avoids the corn silking window.
Opens a summer window for double-crop soybeans or a cover/forage where rain allows.
gaps: Wheat loss costs come from a May-August weather model; fall-to-spring droughts are under-predicted (2023 regional wheat test: $0.23B predicted vs $0.75B actual).
Part of the lower bill comes from lower liability per acre (less insured value).
risks: Wheat usually earns much less per acre than corn here: check the income line.
Winter-kill, head scab in wet springs, and local market access.

irr_high.text: About {irr}% of cropland here is irrigated. Insured drought losses here are mostly on dryland acres: a dryland field likely faces a higher bill than this county average, an irrigated field a much lower one. Yields and loss costs are county averages that mix irrigated and dryland fields (insured sorghum and wheat are mostly dryland, corn often irrigated).

irr_some.text: About {irr}% of cropland here is irrigated; the county average mixes dryland and irrigated acres.

dry_summer.text: Dry summers (June-August rain about {prcp} mm, NASA POWER 1991-2020): a cover crop's spring water use is a real risk here; plan early termination.

hot.text: Hot summers (about {edd} degree-days above 30 C in June-August, NASA POWER 1991-2020): corn rotation benefits shrink in the hottest years.

low_aws.text: Soils here hold little plant-available water (about {aws} mm in the top 150 cm, SSURGO); drought stress builds fast. Check your own field's soils.

ww_drought.text: Winter wheat here is exposed to fall-to-spring drought that the May-August weather model does not see; wheat loss costs are likely understated.

c45.text: Climate projections put this county's drought bill about {c45}% higher around 2045 (SSP2-4.5, NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, today's acres and prices).

wheat_thin.text: Few years of insured wheat in this county: its wheat loss cost leans on state/region patterns.

wheat_pooled.text: No insured wheat here in 2020-2024: the wheat loss cost is a pooled model estimate and the liability per acre is the state's (the US average where the state insures under 10,000 wheat acres, e.g. Iowa, where the usual small grain is oats).

sorghum_thin.text: Few years of insured sorghum in this county: its sorghum loss cost leans on state/region patterns.

sorghum_pooled.text: No insured sorghum here in 2020-2024: sorghum loss cost and liability per acre are state-pooled model estimates.

soybeans_thin.text: Few years of insured soybeans here: the soybean loss cost leans on state/region patterns.
